words.textHint: A professional who designs buildings and draws the plans before construction begins.
A very large and busy city where millions of people live and work.
A building in a foreign country where one nation's official representatives work.
A system where citizens choose their leaders by voting.
The written document that lays out a country's most important rules and rights.
An elected official who writes laws in the upper chamber of a legislature.
The elected leader in charge of one state rather than the whole country.
A country's top official representative sent to live and work in another nation.
A group of ordinary citizens who listen to a trial and decide if someone is guilty.
The final decision announced at the end of a trial.
The public building where trials are held and judges work.
An event where people cast votes to pick their leaders.
The paper or form you mark to cast your vote.
The speeches, ads, and rallies a candidate uses to win votes.
The official status of belonging to a country, with all its rights and duties.
A form of rule where a king or queen holds the throne.
A group of many lands and peoples ruled by one powerful leader.
A settlement in a distant land that is controlled by a faraway mother country.
When the people rise up and overthrow their rulers to start a new government.
An advanced society with cities, writing, laws, and organized culture.
The all-powerful ruler of ancient Egypt, often buried inside a giant tomb.
A fighter in ancient Rome who battled in front of huge crowds in an arena.
A sword-carrying warrior from old Japan who followed a strict code of honor.
A seafaring raider from ancient Scandinavia who sailed in longships.
Describing the era of castles, knights, and kingdoms between ancient and modern times.
The great rebirth of painting, sculpture, and learning in Europe after the Middle Ages.
A piece of land surrounded by water on three sides but still attached to the mainland.
The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, halfway between the poles.
One half of the globe, split by an imaginary line.
A large area of high, flat land that rises above the country around it.
The giant round arena in Rome where ancient crowds watched fierce contests.
A huge ancient statue with a human head and the body of a lion.
A doctor who performs operations by cutting into patients to fix them.
A professional who argues cases in court and gives legal advice.
Someone who investigates news stories and writes reports for the public.
An official who represents their country abroad and negotiates with other nations.
A scientist who digs up ancient objects and ruins to learn about the past.
An emergency worker who treats patients in the vehicle with flashing lights on the way to the hospital.
A professional who prepares and hands out medicines at a drugstore counter.
A tradesperson who installs and fixes the wiring that brings power to your lights.
A senior teacher who lectures students at a university.
A professional who keeps track of a company's money and prepares the financial records.
An expert who studies how the mind works and helps people with their thoughts and emotions.
The branch of math where letters like x and y stand for unknown numbers.
The branch of math about shapes, angles, lines, and circles.
The study of how money, goods, and services move through society.
The outline of a city's tall buildings against the horizon.
A quieter residential neighborhood on the outer edge of a big city.
A wide, grand city street often lined with trees.
A grand and towering church, often with stained glass and tall spires.
A statue or structure built to honor an important person or event.
The domed building where lawmakers meet to pass legislation.
The assembly of elected representatives that makes a nation's laws.
Moving from your home country to settle permanently in a new one.
The fixed amount of money you earn from your job each year.
A temporary position where a student works to gain real experience, often unpaid.
The type of money a country uses, like dollars, euros, or yen.
A sale where people bid against each other and the highest offer wins.
The main office building where a company's top leaders work.
An old object made by humans long ago, often displayed in a museum.
Someone who starts their own company and takes big risks to build it.
When prices keep rising over time so your money buys less than before.
A period when the economy shrinks, businesses struggle, and jobs disappear.
The art of handling relations between countries through talks instead of war.
A slow system of officials, paperwork, and endless forms that runs large organizations.
The academic study of human cultures, societies, and how our species developed.
The study of deep questions about existence, knowledge, and how we should live.
The academic field that studies how groups of people behave and organize themselves.
Biased information spread on purpose to shape public opinion, often by governments.
When authorities block or delete books, news, or speech they do not want people to see.
A paid professional who tries to persuade lawmakers to vote a certain way.
Talking for hours on end in a legislature to delay a vote on a bill.
The formal process of charging a president or official with wrongdoing to remove them from office.
Redrawing voting district borders into odd shapes to give one party an unfair advantage.
When citizens vote directly on a single question or law instead of choosing a leader.
An official change or addition made to a constitution or law.
A leader's power to reject a bill that lawmakers have passed.
Trade and money penalties that countries impose to punish another nation.
A formal written agreement signed between countries, often to end a war.
A nation's full right to govern itself without outside interference.
The person who brings a lawsuit against someone else in court.
An official court order demanding that someone show up to testify or hand over documents.
Proof that a suspect was somewhere else when the crime happened.
An official who watches you sign important documents and stamps them to make them legal.
When one company controls an entire market with no competition, also a famous board game.
The legal state of being unable to pay your debts, forcing a company or person to give up assets.
A long-term bank loan people take out to buy a house.
The share of profits a company pays out to its shareholders.
A tax charged on goods coming into a country from abroad.
Where shares of companies are bought and sold, with prices rising and falling all day.
The total value of everything a country makes and sells in a year, often shortened to three letters.
The basic economic rule that prices rise when many buyers chase few goods.
When a company hires outside workers, often overseas, to do work its own staff used to do.
Someone who works independently for many clients instead of one employer.
The expert who chooses and arranges the pieces displayed in a museum or gallery.
Someone whose profession is drawing and designing maps.
The restaurant expert who recommends which bottle of fermented grape drink pairs with your meal.
A professional who uses statistics to calculate risks for insurance companies.
The doctor who puts you to sleep safely before an operation.
Using lab science like fingerprints and DNA to solve crimes.
A scientist who tracks how diseases spread through populations.
A scientist who studies dinosaur bones and other ancient fossils.
The scientist who studies the atmosphere and predicts tomorrow's rain or sunshine.
The science of designing chairs, desks, and tools to fit the human frame comfortably.
The profession of designing how a city's streets, parks, and neighborhoods fit together.
When wealthy newcomers move into an old neighborhood, raising rents and pushing out longtime residents.
A giant chain of cities that have grown together into one enormous urban region.
A chain or cluster of many islands scattered across the sea.
A narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses, with water on both sides.
A long, narrow sea inlet between steep cliffs, carved by ancient glaciers in places like Norway.
The giant slabs of the Earth's crust that slowly drift and cause earthquakes when they collide.
An imaginary line running from pole to pole used to measure east and west positions.
The hilltop citadel of ancient Athens, crowned with marble temples.
The lost mountain city of the Incas hidden high in the Peruvian Andes.
The gleaming white marble tomb in India that an emperor built for his beloved wife.
The mysterious prehistoric ring of giant standing rocks in England.
The falling-blade machine used for executions during the French Revolution.
The era in American history when making and selling alcohol was banned nationwide.
The decades-long standoff between two superpowers fought with spies and missiles instead of open battles.
The former South African system that legally separated people by race.
